speaker_role: independent counselor (certified educational planner, UC Berkeley college-counseling instructor, founder of Magellan College Counseling)
commercial_incentive: Yes - promotes her paid counseling packages/team and a separate paid webinar on financial aid
key_insights: Per an annual NACAC survey the speaker cites, colleges rank admission factors consistently: grades first, then course rigor, then GPA/rank, then test scores, followed by more subjective factors (recommendations, extracurriculars/leadership, essays)

GPA is generally evaluated as 9th-11th grade, cumulative, and unweighted (an A is an A, a B is a B) at most colleges outside the UC/Cal State systems, and typically counts only the five core academic subjects (math, science, English, foreign language, social studies)

US high school grade distributions have shifted dramatically: speaker cites roughly 40% of US high schoolers graduating with an A average, versus a traditional bell curve decades earlier, intensifying competition for grade-focused selective schools

A school profile document (available on most high school websites) travels with transcripts and gives colleges context on average GPA/scores and which honors/AP courses were available, so rigor is judged relative to that specific school's offerings

Recommends choosing recommenders based on relationship and effort shown (e.g. a hard-earned B from a teacher who saw the effort) rather than only teachers who gave an A, since the actual recommendation form asks about maturity, leadership, and response to setbacks, not just grades

Explains holistic review varies by institution and even by campus within one university system (cites UC Santa Barbara stating roughly 50% academic/50% non-academic, unlike other UC campuses that don't disclose weighting), meaning no single stat guarantees admission

Recommends prioritizing depth of involvement in one to two activities over breadth; leadership can mean taking real responsibility in an existing project, not necessarily founding a club or holding a title

For college list research, advises researching fit (major availability, clubs, size, location, climate) before ever looking at admissions statistics, and specifically flags that low name-recognition does not equal low quality (citing Harvard Law School's list of undergraduate feeder schools, which regularly includes lesser-known institutions)

On cost: notes roughly 25% of aid money nationally comes from the colleges themselves (institutional merit aid), that sticker price is not the real price at most private colleges, and that some top-ranked private colleges do not offer merit aid at all, so families should research which schools do before ruling out options on price
specific_numbers_or_facts: NACAC survey (cited by speaker) ranks grades as the top admissions factor for the past ~10 years, followed by rigor, GPA/rank, then test scores
Speaker states roughly 40% of US high school graduates now have an A average GPA
Cites UC Santa Barbara stating its process is roughly 50% academic / 50% non-academic factors
National average ACT score cited as approximately 19-20 (out of 36)
Cites roughly 25% of college-funding aid nationally coming from institutions' own merit/need-based grants (vs. smaller private scholarships)
Example cited: a student admitted to Kalamazoo/Juniata College with a $30,000/year renewable scholarship
Recommends about one college researched per week during junior year as a manageable research pace
notable_or_distinctive: Uses the Harvard Law School undergraduate-feeder list as a concrete, checkable argument against name-recognition bias when building a college list, and gives a specific worked contrast (UC Santa Barbara's disclosed 50/50 holistic weighting vs. other UC campuses that don't disclose theirs).
reliability_notes: Recorded during the COVID-era test-optional/virtual-visits period (references 'class of 2021/2022/2023' and pandemic-driven policy shifts), so specific testing-policy details (test-optional vs. test-blind at named schools) are dated and have since changed at many institutions (e.g. UC system and others have since reinstated testing); general admissions-factor and financial-aid principles are more durable.
